Equivalence of Virtual Synchronous Machines and
Frequency-Droops for Converter-Based MicroGrids
Salvatore D’Arco and Jon Are Suul, Member, IEEE
Abstract—Over the last decade, frequency-droop-based control
schemes have become the preferred solution in microgrids dominated by power electronic converters. More recently, the concept
of virtual synchronous machines (VSMs) has emerged as an effective method for adding virtual inertia to the power system through
the control of power electronic converters. These two approaches
have been developed in two separate contexts, but present strong
similarities. In fact, they are equivalent under certain conditions,
as demonstrated in this letter. Analysis of this equivalence provides
additional physics-based insight into the tuning and operation of
both types of controllers.

This letter has demonstrated the equivalence between
VSM-based control and frequency-droop controllers. The
demonstrated equivalence links into a single theoretical frame
two well established concepts that have been developed so
far in separate contexts. This provides a new perspective for
the VSM and a deeper physical insight into the interpretation
of the gain and ﬁlter parameters for droop controllers in converter-based microgrids. REFERENCES

A B S T R A C T
As power system renewable energy penetrations increase, the ways in which key renewable technologies such as
wind and solar photovoltaics (PV) differ from thermal generators become more apparent.

increase, the ways in which key renewable technologies such as
wind and solar photovoltaics (PV) differ from thermal generators become more apparent. Many studies have
examined the variability and uncertainty of such generators and described how generation and load can be
balanced for a wide variety of annual energy penetrations, at timescales from seconds to years. Another important characteristic of these resources is asynchronicity, the result of using inverters to interface the prime
energy source with the power system as opposed to synchronous generators. Unlike synchronous generators,
whose frequency of alternating current (AC) injection is physically coupled to the rotation of the machine itself,
inverter based asynchronous generators do not share the same physical coupling with the generated frequency.

inverter based asynchronous generators do not share the same physical coupling with the generated frequency. These subtle differences impact the operations of power systems developed around the characteristics of synchronous generators. In this paper we review current knowledge and open research questions concerning the
interplay between asynchronous inverter-based resources (IBRs) and cycle- to second-scale power system dynamics, with a focus on how stability and control may be impacted or need to be achieved differently when there
are high instantaneous penetrations of IBRs across an interconnection. This work does not seek to provide a
comprehensive review of the latest developments, but is instead intended to be accessible to any reader with an
engineering background and an interest in power systems and renewable energy.

IBR characteristics.

1.1. Converter types and associated energy resources
The largest power systems in the world today were designed around
the physics of synchronous generators or, more generally, synchronous
machine converters (SMCs). Fig. 3 shows the generator portion of an
SMC, with an internal rotor that rotates within the stator coils. The
output, by design, is three AC voltage waveforms equally spaced in
time, with sinusoidal frequencies that depend on the rotational velocity
of the rotor.

put, by design, is three AC voltage waveforms equally spaced in
time, with sinusoidal frequencies that depend on the rotational velocity
of the rotor. This output is shown on the right hand side of Fig. 3. A
natural result of this relationship is that the frequency of the voltage
waveform is tied to the inertial characteristics of the rotor. On the other
hand, IBRs use power electronics to convert the DC output of generation
sources to AC with a frequency that matches the power system, and are
hence asynchronous. The physical characteristics associated with the
AC waveform generated with an IBR are different from those generated
with an SMC; clarifying the differences and implications of this distinction is a primary purpose of this paper.

due to the adoption of renewable energy in the form of wind and solar
PV, it is not the case that converter type (SMC or IBR) maps directly to
whether a generator uses renewable energy or not. Many methods for
converting renewable energy to electricity use SMCs. Hydropower is the
dominant (and longstanding) example, but biomass, geothermal and
concentrating solar power plants also use SMCs to generate electricity. Conversely, battery energy storage and fuel cell technologies are IBRs
that may rely some or completely on non-renewable energy sources. Table 1 provides an overview of the most common sources of energy

2. Power electronic converters
Advances in semiconductor technology and energy-conversion efficiencies of power electronic converters (PECs) during the last few
decades have resulted in the widespread adoption of PECs at various
levels of the power system. At the consumer level, PECs are generally
deployed in the form of DC-to-DC converters for general electronic
devices, or AC-to-DC converters for laptops, computers, and televisions,
to name a few. Large-scale PECs, such as rectifiers and inverters, are
generally used to control the flow of tens of kilowatts to hundreds of
megawatts (or the reactive power equivalent) of power.

transmission level, PECs typically interface variable and uncertain renewable sources, such as solar PV, with the AC power system, resulting
in an asynchronous generation source. The increased integration of
renewable energy sources into the power system consequently leads to
increased PEC penetration, both from an annual energy and instantaneous perspective. PECs have a wide range of applications, and they can generally be

• AC-to-DC converters (rectifiers)
• DC-to-AC converters (inverters)

• AC-to-AC converters

2.2. Basic operation
Solar PV inverters are used for both stand-alone and grid-tied systems. Solar PV panels produce DC power, which must be converted to
AC power to interface with the power system, a process that is accomplished with the inverter. Inverters (or charge controllers, depending on the Solar PV interfacing scheme) commonly incorporate
maximum power point tracking control schemes to achieve optimal
energy production, either directly for the DC-to-AC conversion, or while
charging a battery system. The AC output current generated by the
inverter must have the same frequency and maintain a specified relative
phase with the utility grid AC voltage waveform (60 Hz in the United
States) to accomplish the desired power injection into the power

grounded by the physics of power system devices, in particular SMCs,
which has traditionally focused on three domains of stability: rotor
angle, frequency, and voltage (Kundur et al., 2004).

3.2. Studying stability with high IBR penetrations
In assessing the stability of a power system, the impacts of a perturbation (such as a load imbalance or fault) on the key stability partitions of voltage, frequency, and rotor angle are typically analyzed. Depending on the size of the power imbalance and the physical influence on the network, there are two fundamentally different approaches
in stability analysis: small-signal and large-signal stability.

in stability analysis: small-signal and large-signal stability. The system
load and power flows are changing continuously as the multitudes of
customers adjust their power needs, with these types of changes being

stability during these minor fluctuations is accomplished through a

3.2.1. Small-signal stability
Small-signal stability is a method of assessing stability under small
load and/or generation variations without any physical change to the
network. Since there are no physical changes to the network, a mathematical model can be formulated in the form of differential algebraic
equations and linearized to assess the stability around a steady-state
operating point. All dynamic elements are cast in the form of first-order
differential equations using the state-space model, whereas the network
is approximated algebraically by neglecting the electromagnetic transients associated with power transmission.

is approximated algebraically by neglecting the electromagnetic transients associated with power transmission. When this model is linearized around a steady-state operating point,
a state matrix can be generated and decomposed into eigenvectors and
a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues—the stability of the system can be
determined by the eigenvalues themselves. Generally, a well-defined
system will have an eigenvalue, or pair, associated with a particular
state variable in the system. Participation analysis can be performed to
identify the interplay between various states. Eigenvalues with a negative real part cause a decaying exponential response that goes to zero
over time, which is a general indicator of stability for the affected state. The rate of decay is proportional to the proximity of the eigenvalue real

5. Simulation and modeling
Bulk power systems are complex, large-scale systems. As a result,
direct experimentation is often not possible, and the field relies heavily
on modeling and simulation for verification and validation of new
ideas. The strategies for simulation and modeling are in a state of
flux–like power systems themselves, which are fundamentally changing
with the rapid growth of new generation technologies such as IBRs. This
section first describes the two major types of simulation used for
studying power system dynamics: RMS and electromagnetic transient
(EMT) simulation. Next, general challenges for meaningful simulation
regardless of type are presented.

5.1. RMS simulation
One common approach for simulating large power systems is to
treat the states of the network (currents and voltages) as steady-state
variables. In a real power system, voltages and currents are approximately sinusoidal waveforms of a common system frequency. In the
steady-state network approximation, the network states are represented
by a single complex number, typically expressed using phasor notation,
as shown in Fig. 17. The magnitude of the phasor corresponds to the
magnitude of the waveform, and the phase is measured relative to a
reference that is common to the entire network. This simplification
reduces the system to one of algebraic relationships instead of differential equations.

ence that is common to the entire network. This simplification
reduces the system to one of algebraic relationships instead of differential equations. When these assumptions are met, an iterative solution
method, such as the Newton-Raphson method, can be employed to
solve for the steady-state load flow. General Electric’s PSLF and Siemens’ PSSE are industry standard software packages based on this RMS
technique that are used in industrial practice for steady state load flow
and dynamic simulations, among other software tools. It is common
practice to assume a balanced network in transmission systems and
perform a sequence decomposition of the three phases, taking only the
positive sequence phase for simulation to reduce computational time. In
practice, a simulation step size equivalent to a quarter of a cycle
(~4 ms) is a common choice (Zhu and Hill, 2018).

5.2. Electromagnetic transient programs
EMT programs (EMTPs) are fundamentally different from RMS
programs in that voltages and currents are represented in the time
domain and the transmission network is modeled by differential
equations rather than algebraic equations (Engineering, 2018). Typical
simulation time steps for commercially available EMTPs such as PSCAD
are in the range of 5–50 μs, which are orders of magnitude smaller than
RMS simulation time steps. As a result, EMTPs are able to accurately
model much faster dynamics (Fig. 18). Of course, this added complexity
results in a higher computational burden. Historically, EMTPs were seldom used for large-scale dynamic simulations because of the computational cost.

5.3.1. Modeling distributed generation

structure (inductor-capacitor-inductor filter, three control loops, etc.)

In addition to the technical details about the type of simulation
used, there are many practical considerations to ensure useful modeling. In North America, NERC is responsible for developing models
that can be used by industry and researchers. For example, a NERC
working group developed the DER_A modeling framework, which can
be used to model both utility-scale and residential-scale PV far more
effectively than previous attempts (Green, 2019).

and parameterizing the model appropriately, ensuring a common
modeling framework. For models of specific generating plants, regulatory agencies typically rely on models provided by the plant owner. In Australia, concerns
over commercial sensitivity mean that publicly available PSCAD models
are black boxes with only a few visible parameters (Silva, 2017). This

system are often the most complex and most difficult to model. As
discussed previously, RMS-type simulators are often inadequate in
identifying potential causes of tripping, such as short transient overvoltages, reverse current flow, or loss of PLL synchronism (NERC,

6. Conclusion
The traditional approaches to power system operations are undergoing a transformation as IBR penetrations, both by annual energy and
peak instantaneous power, continue to increase in systems all over the
world. While there are no fundamental hindrances to very high penetrations of IBRs in power systems, they do require amended approaches
to ensure proper stability and operation. The forms these changes need
to take are shaped by the physical differences of SMCs and IBRs. SMC
control and stability is based on the massive, rotational characteristics
of generators, whereas IBRs are built up from power electronic
switches.

of generators, whereas IBRs are built up from power electronic
switches. Because modern power systems were formed around SMCs,
our traditional approaches to stability and control assume large quantities of rotational inertia, which IBRs cannot provide. What IBRs can
provide is fast response (generally faster than SMCs); nonetheless this
difference complicates the large scale integration and control of IBRs in
AC power systems. This paper’s discussion of power electronics, IBR control strategies,
and their stability implications reveals significant potential to mitigate
operational challenges with grid supporting IBRs (e.g., fast-frequency

synchronous or half-synchronous speeds at 3,600 RPM or 1,800 RPM, respectively, where the number of pole pairs serves to multiple the RPM to the
output frequency.

Data-driven control has rapidly matured into a powerful complement to classical model-based paradigms. Among 
the most successful approaches are nonparametric, trajectory-centric methods built on Willems et al.’s fundamen- 
tal lemma and model-free reinforcement learning (RL) schemes. In this survey, we reverse the usual presentation 
order to reﬂect their diﬀering assumptions and scopes. First, this paper provides a uniﬁed treatment of fundamen- 
tal lemma-based methods, which require knowledge of the system structure (LTI or suitably lifted nonlinear) but 
oﬀer rigorous guarantees by replacing explicit model identiﬁcation with input-output trajectory representations.

noisy measurements. This paper then turns to RL-based control, which lifts the structural constraints entirely —

paper also surveys data-driven defense strategies against Denial-of-Service and false-data-injection attacks, from 
anomaly detection to resilient control. To illustrate practical impact, this paper steps through case studies ranging

embedding data-driven models in large-scale optimization for next-generation CPESs.

1. Introduction 
1.1. Cyber-physical energy systems 
With the accelerated development of information and communica- 
tion technologies, a critical mass of instruments and devices with com- 
munication functions has been widely deployed in power systems to en- 
hance state observability, control responsiveness, and operational ﬂex- 
ibility in the face of increased penetration of renewable generation at 
all voltage levels and the mass roll-out of electriﬁcation plans across 
many end-user sectors. This trend is transforming energy systems into 
cyber-physical energy systems (CPESs).

1.2. Reinforcement learning based data-driven control 
Whereas many data-driven approaches estimate a map from data 
to control inputs oﬄine, reinforcement learning (RL), a powerful tool 
within the family of machine learning, embeds policy learning within 
the closed-loop interaction, allowing an agent to stochastically explore 
and adapt to its environment online [11] . By formulating power-system 
control tasks as Markov decision processes (MDPs), RL can discover 
adaptive policies that cope with model uncertainty, unmodeled nonlin- 
earities, and evolving operating conditions [12] . In CPESs, RL-based decision mechanisms have attracted intense in- 
terest as a means to overcome the limitations of ﬁxed, model-based con- 
trollers.

In CPESs, RL-based decision mechanisms have attracted intense in- 
terest as a means to overcome the limitations of ﬁxed, model-based con- 
trollers. For example, RL has been applied to voltage regulation [13–15] , 
state estimation [16–18] , energy management [19] , control of power 
converters [20,21] , and economic dispatch [22] . We refer the readers 
to [23] for more references on RL methods applied to CPESs. These 
RL methods have demonstrated the ability to adapt to unforeseen dis- 
turbances and networked interactions that hamper traditional control 
laws, thus representing a powerful complement to model-based designs 
in large-scale, uncertain CPES environments.

1.3. Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma and direct data-driven control 
Despite the early successes of RL in CPESs, its reliance on large 
amounts of data, signiﬁcant computational resources, and the absence of 
formal stability guarantees limit its deployment in safety-critical infras- 
tructure. In parallel, another data-driven frontier has recently emerged, 
founded on Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma [24] . This result shows 
that, for a controllable linear time-invariant (LTI) system, a single suf- 
ﬁciently rich input-output trajectory spans the entire system behavior 
via linear combinations of its time-shifts. In eﬀect, one can represent 
all admissible future trajectories with a nonparametric, trajectory-based 
formulation.

combinations of its time-shifts. In eﬀect, one can represent 
all admissible future trajectories with a nonparametric, trajectory-based 
formulation. Inspired by this work, a number of applications and generaliza- 
tions have been developed, including state-feedback and robust control 
[25–29] , data-driven MPC [30–33] , nonlinear system control [34,35] , 
and data-driven state estimation [36–38] . Although these techniques are 
still maturing, early applications in CPES contexts —such as data-driven 
voltage regulation, fault detection, and grid synchronization —are al- 
ready emerging [37,39,40] . By circumventing explicit system identi- 
ﬁcation, the fundamental lemma framework promises scalable, theo- 
retically grounded solutions to the high-dimensional, uncertain, and 
network-induced complexities of modern CPESs.

1.4. Outline of this survey 
The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section 6 re- 
views a widely used deep reinforcement learning(DRL) framework. Sections 2 –8 then present a comprehensive survey of fundamental 
lemma-based data-driven methods, spanning theoretical developments 
and their potential applications in CPESs. Speciﬁcally, in Section 2 , we 
examine data-driven feedback controller synthesis for LTI systems, cov- 
ering both noise-free and noise-corrupted data scenarios. Section 3 con- 
tinues by exploring recent extensions to nonlinear dynamics, highlight- 
ing key techniques such as lifting, immersion, and interpolation.

2. Data-driven feedback control for LTI systems 
To provide a solid foundation for tackling more complex problems, 
this section focuses on the essential model class of LTI systems. Our goal 
is to control such systems using pre-collected measurement data. We 
begin by introducing a basic data-driven framework that utilizes exact 
(noise-free) and measured (noisy) input-state data, followed by imple- 
mentations based on noise-free and noisy input-output data. Finally, we 
review applications of this approach in addressing several classic prob- 
lems in control theory.

2.5. Summary and outlook 
In this section, we reviewed a suite of fundamental lemma-based 
methods for data-driven feedback control of LTI systems. Starting from 
exact input-state trajectories, we demonstrated how to compute state- 
feedback gains via a data-dependent LMI. We then extended these re- 
sults to accommodate noisy input-state data through slack variables and 
robust formulations. Next, we relaxed the requirement for state mea- 
surements by employing input-output data and further addressed mea- 
surement noise with regularization techniques. Finally, we surveyed sev- 
eral important extensions, including optimal control, online implemen- 
tation, robust control, dissipativity, distributed control and aperiodic 
control.

important extensions, including optimal control, online implemen- 
tation, robust control, dissipativity, distributed control and aperiodic 
control. Together, these developments show that fundamental lemma-based 
controllers can recover classical objectives, e.g., stability, optimality, 
and robustness, in a fully data-driven fashion. However, their inher- 
ent reliance on linear dynamics limits applicability in CPES components 
with strong nonlinear behavior. This motivates the transition in the next 
section to data-driven methods that explicitly address nonlinear system 
dynamics.

tees for LTI systems, their performance can deteriorate when confronted 
with the pronounced nonlinearities of many CPES components.

3.4. Extensions 
Besides methods reviewed in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 , recent work 
has linked nonlinear data-driven systems with linear parameter-varying 
(LPV) systems [85] , input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis [86] , and state- 
dependent representations [87] . Compared with numerous eﬀorts made 
in the LTI case in Section 2.4 , many avenues remain open for future ex- 
ploration.

4. Data-driven predictive control 
The previous sections introduced data-driven feedback controllers 
for both LTI and nonlinear systems. In traditional control theory, model 
predictive control (MPC) plays a central role due to its ability to han- 
dle multivariable systems, explicitly incorporate constraints, and opti- 
mize system performance over a prediction horizon. Its eﬀectiveness 
has been widely demonstrated in diverse real-world applications, rang- 
ing from industrial chemical process control, where safety and eﬃciency 
are paramount, to high-precision tasks such as UAV trajectory tracking 
[88] , where dynamic environments and physical limitations must be ac- 
counted for in real time. Therefore, in contrast to the feedback control 
methods discussed earlier, another popular research direction is the ap- 
plication of data-driven approaches to MPC.

6.2. DRL in CPES 
In cyber-physical energy systems, DRL oﬀers a distinct advantage 
over traditional optimization and control techniques by enabling sys- 
tems to learn optimal policies through continuous interaction with com- 
plex and uncertain environments. This capability is particularly well- 
suited to the dynamic, distributed, and data-intensive characteristics of 
modern energy systems. As CPES increasingly integrates renewable en- 
ergy sources, energy storage, and advanced digital control mechanisms, 
DRL has emerged as a powerful tool to enhance system ﬂexibility, re- 
silience, and operational eﬃciency.

6.3. Summary and outlook 
In summary, DRL provides a fully model-free framework for tack- 
ling high-dimensional, nonlinear CPES control tasks — such as voltage 
regulation under uncertainty — by learning policies directly from in- 
teraction data. However, both DRL and the fundamental lemma-based 
data-driven methods reviewed earlier assume that online measurements 
and control commands are reliable and untampered. In practice, CPES 
networks are vulnerable to adversarial cyber-physical attacks that can 
corrupt or block these data streams.

7.1. DoS attacks 
DoS attacks are designed to disrupt data availability, typically by 
jamming or ﬂooding communication channels with malicious traﬃc 
[120] . In CPESs, such interruptions may occur along (i) the link between 
remote terminal units (RTUs) or phasor measurement units (PMUs) and 
the control center, and (ii) the link between the control center and gener- 
ator governors. By blocking measurement updates or delaying actuator 
commands, DoS attacks can severely degrade system performance and 
precipitate instability. In what follows, we ﬁrst review data-driven detection methods and 
then turn to resilient control strategies.

7.1.1. Detection via RL 
As a strong technique in obtaining optimal action policies in diﬀer- 
ent domains, RL approaches have shown promise in learning optimal 
detection and mitigation policies under varying DoS scenarios: 
• DRL framework: [131] developed a DRL-based framework that 
learned to mitigate distributed DoS ﬂooding in real time by dynam- 
ically adapting its policy to evolving attack patterns. 
• Model-free RL for POMDPs: [122] cast the DoS detection problem as a 
partially observable markov decision process (POMDPs) and applied 
model-free RL to derive a robust, universal detection algorithm. 
• Recursive CNN-enhanced Q-learning: [123] proposed an anti-jamming 
algorithm using Q-learning with a recursive convolutional neural 
network to extract temporal features from spectrum-waterfall data 
for enhanced detection.

7.3. Extensions 
While the preceding subsections have surveyed data-driven detec- 
tion and resilient control techniques for DoS and FDI attacks individ- 
ually, real-world adversaries may deploy coordinated [155] or hybrid 
attack [156] strategies that interleave multiple attack vectors to evade 
single-mode countermeasures. For instance, an attacker might brieﬂy 
ﬂood communication channels (which is a type of DoS attacks) to force 
the system into open-loop operation, then inject stealthy false data (FDI) 
into the next available measurement batch to maximize disruption. To extend our resilient control framework to such compound threats, 
we propose the following directions:

7.3.1. Summary and outlook 
In this section, we surveyed data-driven strategies for detecting and 
mitigating DoS and FDI attacks in CPESs. Detection methods ranged 
from RL-based jamming classiﬁers to adaptive residual and fundamen- 
tal lemma monitors, while resilient control schemes included predic- 
tive controllers with slack variables, ADP-based regulation, and time- 
varying feedback laws. We also proposed extensions for coordinated or 
hybrid attacks via composite detectors, attack-aware slack scheduling, 
and mode-switching policies. Building on these developments, the next 
section presents real-world CPES applications to illustrate the practical 
performance of the reviewed control, estimation, and security methods.

have spurred the integration of renewables, eﬃciency measures, storage 
solutions, and demand-side management into modern power systems. CPESs, which seamlessly fuse energy-process dynamics with sensing, 
communication, and real-time computation, oﬀer a promising platform 
for addressing the uncertainties of renewable generation and the oper- 
ational challenges of large, geographically distributed grids.

In this survey, we have chronicled the rapid evolution of data- 
driven control for CPESs, beginning with nonparametric, trajectory-

based methods grounded in Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma. We ﬁrst 
detailed how these methods —requiring an LTI or suitably lifted system 
representation —enable state-feedback synthesis in linear and nonlinear 
settings, extend naturally to model predictive control, and support non- 
parametric state estimation under both noise-free and noisy conditions. We then reviewed RL approaches, which lift structural constraints en- 
tirely and learn control policies directly from interaction data, trading 
formal stability proofs for broad applicability to complex and uncertain 
grid dynamics.

formal stability proofs for broad applicability to complex and uncertain 
grid dynamics. Building on these control and estimation foundations, 
we turned to CPES-speciﬁc challenges by surveying data-driven defense 
strategies against DoS and FDI attacks, from anomaly detection to re- 
silient controller design. Finally, to illustrate practical impact, we ex- 
amined a series of case studies, from canonical generator benchmarks 
to high-ﬁdelity, grid-connected wind-turbine simulations, showcasing 
how both trajectory-based controllers and RL agents can meet the scale, 
complexity, and uncertainties of modern power networks. Looking ahead, several research avenues stand out as particularly 
fertile: 
• Learning-augmented data-driven methods.

nties of modern power networks. Looking ahead, several research avenues stand out as particularly 
fertile: 
• Learning-augmented data-driven methods. By embedding RL 
[23,160] or other learning agents around fundamental lemma- 
based inner loops, one can leverage live operational data to 
reﬁne policies or value functions while retaining provable sta- 
bility and performance certiﬁcates. Such hybrid schemes hold 
promise for large-scale, time-varying CPES tasks, i.e., from load- 
frequency regulation to voltage security, oﬀering faster adaptation 
under nonstationary conditions without sacriﬁcing theoretical 
rigor. 
• Core CPES control problems. Although foundational tasks such as volt- 
age regulation and frequency stabilization have been addressed us- 
ing RL-based data-driven approaches [161] , they remain ripe for fun- 
damental lemma-based data-driven treatment.

• Network-induced phenomena. Beyond the cyber-threats we have re- 
viewed in Section 7 , CPESs also face with communication delays, 
packet drops, and topology changes. Extending data-driven tools, 
especially those inherently robust to aperiodic sampling or adver-

security.

• Topology inference and integration. The geographically distributed na- 
ture of CPESs gives rise to complex interaction networks. Recent 
causality-based methods proposed in [163] can infer network topol- 
ogy from a single trajectory, providing valuable insight into system 
behavior. Integrating topology inference with data-driven control 
promises to improve performance by tailoring algorithms to the true 
underlying structure. 
• Optimization integration. Beyond real-time control and estimation, 
CPES operation hinges on solving large optimization problems, such 
as optimal power ﬂow [164] , economic dispatch [22] , and demand 
response [165] . Embedding nonparametric, data-driven plant mod- 
els into convex or distributed optimization frameworks promises to 
accelerate decision-making and improve scalability. 
• Bridging theory and practice.

s into convex or distributed optimization frameworks promises to 
accelerate decision-making and improve scalability. 
• Bridging theory and practice. While countless algorithms have 
been born in simulation, real-world validation on e.g., hardware 
testbeds, microgrids, or utility pilots, remains urgent. Deploying 
data-driven controllers in these environments will expose practi- 
cal issues of robustness, computational tractability, and legacy- 
system interoperability, thereby closing the loop between theory and 
application. By pursuing these directions, the control community can not only 
deepen the theoretical foundations of data-driven methods but also de- 
liver the adaptive, resilient, and eﬃcient solutions that tomorrow’s en- 
ergy systems demand.

1. Introduction
The future of the global energy system is deeply uncertain, and the choices that 
are made in the coming years will have enormous consequences for the future of 
the climate and, indeed, human civilization. To understand how our energy system 
is changing, each year a variety of organizations produce long-term projections 
that imagine a wide range of futures based on divergent visions about policies, 
technologies, prices, and geopolitics. Because these projections vary widely and depend heavily on their varied assumptions 
and methodologies, they are difficult to compare on an apples-to-apples basis.

2. Key Findings
At the 28th Conference of the Parties (COP28) to the United Nations Framework 
Convention on Climate Change held in Dubai, world leaders agreed to “transitioning 
away from fossil fuels in the energy system.”11 Some advocates, governments, and 
civil society figures have critiqued this agreement and argued instead for the total 
phaseout of fossil fuels to achieve long-term climate goals. However, all scenarios 
examined here, including those consistent with limiting warming to 1.5°C by 2100, show 
substantial global fossil fuel consumption through at least 2050, suggesting that a 
phaseout is not a prerequisite to achieving international climate goals.

tial global fossil fuel consumption through at least 2050, suggesting that a 
phaseout is not a prerequisite to achieving international climate goals. As we have noted in previous Global Energy Outlooks,12 world primary energy demand 
has experienced a series of energy additions, not energy transitions, with newer 
technologies such as nuclear, wind, and solar building on top of incumbent sources 
such as biomass, coal, oil, and natural gas. To achieve international climate goals and 
limit warming to 1.5°C or 2°C by 2100, a true energy transition is needed. But does 
achieving such goals require phasing out fossil fuels entirely? The scenarios we analyze in this report suggest that the answer is no.

If fossil fuels are not phased out of the energy system, limiting warming to international 
climate targets implies a substantial scale-up of carbon removal technologies, including 
direct air capture (DAC), bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (CCS), and naturebased solutions, all of which will require robust monitoring, reporting, and verification.

As the global economy becomes more energy efficient, world primary energy demand 
grows slowly or declines under almost all scenarios examined here. This trend is seen 
most clearly in Ambitious Climate scenarios, where aggregate energy demand declines 
by as much as 33 percent (Equinor Bridges). Falling energy demand occurs primarily in 
high-income countries, with continued growth in energy consumption in many low-income 
nations. Some scenarios, such as the IEA’s NZE, highlight how expanding access to modern 
energy services in low-income regions can be consistent with declining global energy 
demand and achieving long-term sustainability goals.

remained roughly flat, declining modestly from 2010 through today. In the decades 
ahead, carbon intensity is projected to continue this modest decline under Reference 
and most Evolving Policies scenarios. Achieving ambitious climate goals, however, will 
require an unprecedented reduction in the carbon intensity of energy.

growth across multiple technologies, particularly wind and solar. Three Ambitious

but these scenarios are not based on existing or announced policies, highlighting the 
need for enhanced policy ambition if nations are to achieve their COP28 renewable 
energy goals. In 2010, renewable electricity was dominated by hydropower, which accounted 
for more than 75 percent of installed capacity worldwide.

At COP28, 22 nations committed to tripling their nuclear energy capacity by 2050. Achieving 
this goal would require a fundamental change in the trajectory of nuclear energy for 
developed nations, as 12 of the 22 experienced declining nuclear energy production from 2012 
through 2022, while 5 currently produce no nuclear power.19 In recent years, nuclear energy 
growth has been led by China and India. Although neither of these countries was part of the 
announcement at COP28, they were the top two nations for nuclear power plant construction 
as of December 2023.20 Globally, nuclear capacity is projected to grow modestly under most 
scenarios, and 2022 levels triple by 2050 in just two scenarios, both from Enerdata.

Depending on how it is produced, rapid growth in global hydrogen demand could extend 
the life of fossil fuels considerably. The oil and gas industry is experienced in producing 
hydrogen through steam methane reforming—the primary means of global production—

3.3.2. Copper
Copper is a fundamental enabler of all aspects of the electricity sector. Its production 
and refining are more diversified than most other minerals discussed in this section, 
with major producers including Chile, Peru, Congo, China, the United States, and 
Russia,52 although more than 40 percent of all processing occurs in China.49
Figure 18 shows the projections for global copper demand. From 1980 to 2022, demand 
grew at an average rate of 8 percent per year. Under projections from IEA, the average 
annual growth rate from 2022 to 2050 slows to between 5 and 6 percent across 
scenarios. Shell and bp, however, project considerably more rapid demand growth, 
increasing by a minimum of 8 percent per year (Shell Archipelagos) and as rapidly as 
14 percent per year through 2040 (bp Net Zero).

3.3.3. Lithium
Like cobalt, global lithium demand rises from a very small base in the years ahead, 
particularly under Ambitious Climate scenarios, to support the deployment of batteries 
in electric vehicles and other applications. Current production is centered in Australia 
and Chile, although continued exploration has led to recent announcements of major 
new deposits, including in the United States.53 
Figure 19 shows the projections for global lithium demand. From 2000 to 2022, demand 
grew on average by 31 percent annually.

Figure 19 shows the projections for global lithium demand. From 2000 to 2022, demand 
grew on average by 31 percent annually. Looking to 2050, the annual growth rate slows 
to 19 percent under IEA STEPS but rises by 27 to 40 percent per year across other 
scenarios from IEA and bp. The fastest growth rate (91 percent annually) comes from 
Shell’s Sky, where demand grows to nearly 3 billion metric tons per year by 2050. Like other minerals discussed in this section, material substitution could substantially 
slow future demand for lithium. Although a wide variety of alternative battery 
chemistries have been under development for years, it is unclear whether, to what 
extent, and over what time frame they will grow to compete with the still-evolving 
lithium-ion chemistries.54

3.3.5. Other Minerals
Although the four minerals discussed in the previous subsections are some of the 
most significant in terms of scale, their rate of clean energy–related demand growth 
is dwarfed by that of other clean energy minerals (Figure 21). While demand for 
lithium grows by roughly one order of magnitude under most of the bp, IEA, and 
Shell scenarios, demand for gallium—which is used in semiconductors and other 
electronics—rises by nearly three orders of magnitude by 2040 under IEA’s scenarios. Demand for vanadium, which today is used in specialized steelmaking and other 
industrial applications, grows fastest in all these scenarios, rising by nearly five orders 
of magnitude by 2040.

extraordinary rates of growth. For example, the USGS reports that global production of

4.  Data and Methods
In this paper, we examined projections energy outlooks from a wide range of sources 
representing a diverse set of views on the future of energy (see Table 1).

assumes no major policy changes; (2) Evolving Policies, which incorporates the 
modeling team’s expectations of policy trends; and (3) scenarios that do not fall into 
one of the other two categories and are typically based on policy targets or technology 
assumptions. We focus on Ambitious Climate scenarios, a major subset of category 3.

4.1. Harmonization

and markets produce useful variation among outlooks, allowing analysts to view 
a wide range of potential energy futures. However, outlooks also have important 
methodological differences, which can complicate direct comparisons and reduce the 
ability to draw insights. One major difference is the choice of reporting units. For primary energy, outlooks 
use different energy units, such as QBtu, million tonnes of oil equivalent (mtoe), 
or exajoules (EJ). In this report, we standardize all units to QBtu.

A second key difference among outlooks is that assumptions about the energy content 
in a given physical unit of fuel result in different conversion factors between data 
presented in energy units (e.g., QBtu) and those presented in physical units (e.g., mbd 
or bcm). Among the outlooks we examine, these assumptions vary by up to 10 percent. Although conversion unit variations may appear small, they are amplified when applied 
across the massive scale of global energy systems, particularly over long time horizons. A third major difference results from varying decisions about including nonmarketed 
biomass, such as locally gathered wood and dung, in historical data and projections 
for primary energy consumption.

ions about including nonmarketed 
biomass, such as locally gathered wood and dung, in historical data and projections 
for primary energy consumption. In previous years, bp and the EIA had not included 
these sources in their projections. However, bp’s Energy Outlook 2023 does include 
nonmarketed biomass, allowing for enhanced comparability. (The EIA publishes its 
International Energy Outlook every two years and did not publish one in 2023.) 
Yet another difference relates to comparing the energy content of fossil and 
nonfossil fuels. The primary energy content of oil, natural gas, and coal is relatively 
well understood and similar across outlooks. However, a substantial portion of that 
embodied energy is wasted as heat during combustion.

The rapid integration of renewable energy sources into the power grid has resulted in the
high utilization of power-electronics devices and operating power systems where inverter-based resources
are dominated. Such a transition has led to a reduction of inertia and system strength. In recent research,
grid-forming converters (GFM) are introduced and developed to alleviate the grid-following converter (GFL)
functionalities and to address the limitations concerning grid support capability, stability, and synchronization
issues.

id-following converter (GFL)
functionalities and to address the limitations concerning grid support capability, stability, and synchronization
issues. However, the efﬁcacy of GFM technology is still under investigation, and the level at which GFM
converters can replace traditional GFLs is still under question. This article aims to bridge the gap in
literature by revisiting the up-to-date research on the capabilities and the limitations of the proposed GFM
converters compared to the traditionally utilized GFL converters, allowing a better understanding of the
current status and future requirements. This includes the GFM converter’s topologies and their performance
for small- and large-signal stability issues, the GFM converters’ ability to enhance grid synchronization,
and transient stability performances.

for small- and large-signal stability issues, the GFM converters’ ability to enhance grid synchronization,
and transient stability performances. Furthermore, the challenges and limitations of the dynamic behavior
of GFM converters from the point of view of fault ride through (FRT) capability, including grid codes and
FRT requirements, FRT methods of GFM converters, postfault behavior, and open research directions, are

Abstract—With an increasing capacity in the converter-based
generation to the modern power system, a growing demand for
such systems to be more grid-friendly has emerged. Consequently,
grid-forming converters have been proposed as a promising solution as they are compatible with the conventional synchronousmachine-based power system.

grid-forming converters have been proposed as a promising solution as they are compatible with the conventional synchronousmachine-based power system. However, most research focuses
on the grid-forming control during normal operating conditions
without considering the fundamental distinction between a gridforming converter and a synchronous machine when considering
its short-circuit capability. The current limitation of grid-forming
converters during fault conditions is not well described in the
available literature and present solutions often aim to switch
the control structure to a grid-following structure during the
fault. Yet, for a future converter-based power system with no
or little integration of synchronous machines, the converters
need to preserve their voltage-mode characteristics and be robust
toward weak-grid conditions.

discusses the fundamental issue of grid-forming converter control
during grid fault conditions and proposes a fault-mode controller

Grid-forming converters are becoming increasingly attractive as potential candidates for converter control of future
power electronics-based power systems due to their gridfriendly functionalities. As the converter include currentsensitive semiconductor devices, it cannot sustain the behavior
of a voltage source during grid faults as its short-circuit
capability is much lower than that of a synchronous generator.

cannot sustain the behavior
of a voltage source during grid faults as its short-circuit
capability is much lower than that of a synchronous generator. This article discusses the issues of current limitation of
grid-forming converters and introduces a proposed method,
which includes several advantageous properties: instantaneous
limitation of the converter currents, compliance with grid code
requirements, and circumvention to switch the fundamentals
of the control structure during the fault. To that end, enhanced
fault recovery is attained by a proposed dynamic virtual
damping controller. With this, it is shown that the grid-forming
converter can provide grid-supporting functionalities during
normal operating conditions and by only modifying the outer
power reference generation instead of the inner structure, fault
ride-through capability is achieved.
